## Why TikTok?

TikTok's For You Page (FYP) is arguably the most influential recommender deployed
in the past decade. Unlike Amazon (item-to-item collaborative filtering) or the
NYT (collaborative topic modeling over articles), TikTok built its product
*around* the recommender — there is no meaningful homepage without it. That
makes it an unusually clean object of study.

## Scenario Design — Two Lenses

Temkin's framework asks three questions: **Who are the users? What are their
key goals? How can we help them accomplish those goals?** TikTok genuinely has
two distinct customer sets, so the analysis is run twice.

### Lens 1 — The end user (viewer / creator)

| Question | Viewer | Creator |
|---|---|---|
| Who? | A scroller opening the app for entertainment, often <30s of attention | Someone posting short video hoping to be seen |
| Key goal? | "Show me something I'll enjoy *right now*, with no work from me" | Reach the right audience without needing followers |
| How does the system help? | Cold-start onboarding asks for interest categories; every swipe is an implicit label that retrains the feed continuously | An "interest graph" instead of a social graph means a brand-new account can go viral if early viewers complete the video |

### Lens 2 — TikTok / ByteDance the organization

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Who is the "user"? | The platform itself, plus advertisers buying against attention |
| Key goal? | Maximize session length and retention, which compounds into ad inventory and creator supply |
| How does the system help? | A real-time training loop (see *Monolith*, below) lets the model chase trends within hours instead of days, keeping the feed feeling "fresh" |

The two lenses are not always aligned — the platform's optimization for watch
time can pull against the viewer's stated goal of "time well spent." This is
the central tension I return to in my recommendations.

## Reverse-Engineering the System

Combining TikTok's own [Newsroom post](https://newsroom.tiktok.com/en-us/how-tiktok-recommends-videos-for-you)
with the publicly released *Monolith* paper ([Liu et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.07663))
and reporting on the WSJ "TikTok investigation," the pipeline appears to be:

1. **Candidate generation.** Filter the catalog down to videos matching the
   viewer's interest embeddings, language, and region. Follower count is
   explicitly *not* a ranking signal.
2. **Prediction.** For each candidate, predict probabilities of like, share,
   comment, follow, *and* — most heavily — completion / rewatch. Watch-time on
   the first ~3 seconds is the dominant early signal.
3. **Ranking.** Combine predictions into a single score; demote near-duplicates
   and back-to-back same-creator/same-sound videos to preserve diversity.
4. **Online training.** Unlike a typical batch system, *Monolith* updates
   embeddings in near real-time using a collisionless hash table (cuckoo
   hashing) with expirable, frequency-filtered entries. This is what makes the
   FYP feel like it "knows you" within ~20 swipes.

Compared to Amazon's item-to-item CF (Linden et al., 2003), TikTok inverts the
problem: Amazon assumed sparse but stable preferences, while TikTok assumes
dense, *non-stationary* preferences ("concept drift") and engineers around it.

## Recommendations to Improve the System

1. **Expose a "why am I seeing this?" panel with editable signals.** Today the
   only viewer-facing controls are *Not Interested* and *Refresh Feed*. Letting
   users see and remove the top contributing signals (e.g., "you watched 3
   skincare videos to completion last Tuesday") would address well-documented
   "rabbit hole" complaints without sacrificing personalization.
2. **Introduce a satiation penalty separate from diversity.** The current
   diversity layer prevents *back-to-back* repetition but not *session-level*
   over-fit. A user who watched 40 minutes of one topic should see the
   recommender's confidence in that topic decay, not compound.
3. **Treat creators as a second optimization target, not just a supply.**
   Surfacing newer creators with high completion rates earlier in their
   distribution curve would diversify the supply side and reduce the platform's
   dependence on a small group of mega-creators — a known fragility for
   ad-supported platforms.
4. **Add an explicit "long-form interest" signal.** TikTok now hosts videos up
   to 10 minutes, but the ranking model is still anchored to short-video
   completion behavior. A separate head predicting long-form completion would
   let the system grow into YouTube-adjacent use cases without retraining the
   primary objective.
